contradictions.topic: Which load state to gate the full-screen (initial) loader on
contradictions.claimA: Gate the full-screen initial loader directly on the combined `loadState.refresh`: `when (articles.loadState.refresh) { is LoadState.Loading -> CircularProgressIndicator(...) }`.
contradictions.claimB: Explicitly says do NOT gate on the combined `loadState.refresh`; gate on `loadState.source.refresh` + `itemCount == 0`, because the combined `loadState.refresh` flips to `NotLoading` before Room finishes writing and drops the spinner a frame early.
contradictions.evidence: ahmed: /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/everything-claude-code-mobile/skills/pagination-patterns/SKILL.md lines 168-172 ('when (articles.loadState.refresh) { is LoadState.Loading -> { CircularProgressIndicator(...) }'). rcosteira: /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/android-skills/plugins/android-skills/skills/paging/SKILL.md line 55 ('Gate the full-screen loader on `loadState.source.refresh` + `itemCount == 0` — not the combined `loadState.refresh`...'). These are directly opposing on the same technical point. Nuance: ahmed's snippet sits in a network-only PagingSource section where source.refresh == refresh, but ahmed also documents RemoteMediator/offline-first (lines 200-259); applied there ahmed's loader pattern is exactly what rcosteira warns against, and when both skills merge into one plugin an agent sees both rules on the same paging code.

bugs.description: CursorArticlePagingSource.load() catches the broad `Exception` and returns LoadResult.Error(e), which swallows kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException. Cancelling the load (e.g. flatMapLatest switching on a new search query, or config change) is turned into a paging Error state instead of propagating cancellation, breaking structured concurrency and showing a spurious error/retry UI.
bugs.evidence: Lines 74-76: `} catch (e: Exception) { LoadResult.Error(e) }`. Contrast with the CORRECT pattern in the same file at lines 40-44 where ArticlePagingSource catches only IOException and HttpException, letting CancellationException propagate. The cursor source violates that pattern.

bugs.description: ArticleRemoteMediator.load() catches the broad `Exception` and returns MediatorResult.Error(e), swallowing CancellationException the same way. On cancellation the mediator reports an error instead of allowing cooperative cancellation.
bugs.evidence: Lines 245-247: `} catch (e: Exception) { MediatorResult.Error(e) }`. Same anti-pattern as the cursor source; should catch specific IOException/HttpException (as done at lines 40-44) and let CancellationException through.

bugs.description: The PaginatedList composable renders the list TWICE inside the same Box: once via ArticleLazyColumn(articles) in the loadState.refresh == NotLoading branch, and again via ArticleLazyColumn(articles) inside PullToRefreshBox. Both are direct children of the same Box, so two LazyColumns stack and overlap on screen. It also double-reads the paging items and the empty/error states are hidden behind the second list.
bugs.evidence: Lines 164-197: the `when (articles.loadState.refresh)` block's NotLoading branch calls `ArticleLazyColumn(articles = articles)` (lines 180-186), and immediately after, `PullToRefreshBox(...) { ArticleLazyColumn(articles = articles) }` (lines 190-196) renders it a second time in the same Box. The pull-to-refresh should wrap the single list, not duplicate it.

bugs.description: In ArticleRemoteMediator, the LoadType.REFRESH network call uses `state.config.pageSize` (20) rather than `state.config.initialLoadSize` for the first page. Paging's initial refresh expects up to initialLoadSize items (defaults to 3x pageSize when unset), so the mediator under-fetches on first load and triggers an immediate extra APPEND.
bugs.evidence: Line 228: `val response = api.getArticles(page = page, pageSize = state.config.pageSize)`. The offline Pager at line 254 uses `PagingConfig(pageSize = 20)` with no initialLoadSize override, so initialLoadSize defaults to 60 while REFRESH only requests 20. RemoteMediator should honor initialLoadSize for the REFRESH load type.

bugs.description: Internal inconsistency: PagingConfig sets enablePlaceholders = false, but the LazyColumn item body handles the null (placeholder) case with ArticlePlaceholder(), and Best Practices advises 'Show shimmer placeholders during initial load'. With placeholders disabled, Paging does not emit null placeholder items, so the ArticlePlaceholder null-branch is effectively dead code and the guidance about placeholders does not match the config.
bugs.evidence: enablePlaceholders = false at line 92; the null-handling branch `if (article != null) { ArticleCard(...) } else { ArticlePlaceholder() }` at lines 139-143; Best Practices 'Show shimmer placeholders during initial load' at line 394. Either enablePlaceholders must be true for the placeholder branch to fire, or the null-branch/advice should be removed.

contradictions.topic: How to collect the one-shot effects/side-effects Channel in Compose (lifecycle scoping)
contradictions.claimA: mvi-architecture collects the side-effects Channel in a plain, non-lifecycle-scoped LaunchedEffect(Unit) that keeps collecting even while the screen is backgrounded.
contradictions.claimB: android-dev explicitly mandates collecting the effects Channel lifecycle-scoped via repeatOnLifecycle so that effects buffer while backgrounded and replay on resume instead of firing off-screen.
contradictions.evidence: Both agree the effect stream is a Channel(Channel.BUFFERED).receiveAsFlow(), so the ONLY divergence is the collection site. ahmed mvi-architecture/SKILL.md:120-128 -> `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.sideEffects.collect { effect -> when(effect){...NavigateToDetail...} } }` (no repeatOnLifecycle). rcosteira android-dev/SKILL.md:57 -> "Collect it in a LaunchedEffect (lifecycle-scoped via repeatOnLifecycle), never collectAsStateWithLifecycle: an effect emitted while the screen is backgrounded buffers and replays on resume instead of being dropped", and the example at lines 90-99 uses `lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { viewModel.effects.collect {...} }`. ahmed's plaint collector defeats the very buffering rationale rcosteira gives and delivers navigation/snackbar while the screen is not visible.

contradictions.topic: Where the initial data load is triggered (UI composable vs ViewModel init)
contradictions.claimA: mvi-architecture triggers the initial load from the UI: LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.onIntent(HomeIntent.LoadItems) } inside the composable.
contradictions.claimB: android-patterns triggers the initial load inside the ViewModel via an init { loadData() } block.
contradictions.evidence: Two ahmed skills that both auto-trigger on ViewModel/Compose code give opposing patterns for the same decision. mvi-architecture/SKILL.md:131-133 -> `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.onIntent(HomeIntent.LoadItems) }`. android-patterns/SKILL.md:107-109 -> `init { loadData() }`. These behave differently across configuration change: init{} runs once per ViewModel (survives rotation), whereas LaunchedEffect(Unit) re-runs when the activity/composition is recreated, re-issuing the load on every rotation.

contradictions.topic: Default dependency-injection framework for greenfield ViewModel/Compose code
contradictions.claimA: Both ahmed skills use Koin unconditionally as the default (koinViewModel()).
contradictions.claimB: House default is Hilt + KSP (hiltViewModel()), with Koin used only when the project already uses Koin.
contradictions.evidence: ahmed mvi-architecture/SKILL.md:112 and android-patterns/SKILL.md:127 -> `viewModel: HomeViewModel = koinViewModel()`. rcosteira android-dev/SKILL.md:20 -> "DI: Hilt + KSP (or android-skills:koin when the project uses Koin)" and the greenfield example at line 87 -> `viewModel: FooViewModel = hiltViewModel()`. On a new project both skills auto-trigger and emit opposing DI setup (Koin vs Hilt). rcosteira hedges by permitting Koin, so this is a divergent default rather than an absolute prohibition, but the greenfield output still conflicts.

bugs.description: The retry() higher-order function is declared as a plain (non-suspend) function but calls delay(1000) and invokes a suspend lambda block(); this does not compile.
bugs.evidence: Lines 156-165: `fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: suspend () -> T): T { repeat(times - 1) { try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { delay(1000) } } return block() }`. Both `block()` (typed `suspend () -> T`) and `delay(1000)` (a suspend function) can only be called from a coroutine or another suspend function. The signature must be `suspend fun retry(...)`. As written the compiler rejects it: 'Suspend function delay should be called only from a coroutine or another suspend function'. It is presented under a `// ✅` heading as a recommended pattern.

bugs.description: retry() catches Exception, which swallows CancellationException and breaks structured concurrency: the loop keeps retrying (and delaying) after its coroutine scope is cancelled.
bugs.evidence: Lines 160-163: `try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { delay(1000) }`. CancellationException is an Exception, so a cancelled block() is caught and the function retries instead of propagating cancellation. Correct form rethrows CancellationException (or catches a narrower type). Ironically rcosteira android-dev/SKILL.md:140 cites exactly this: `// rethrow first — a broad catch would swallow CancellationException`.

bugs.description: fetchUser() wraps a suspend network call in runCatching, which catches Throwable including CancellationException, so a cancelled call is converted to Result.failure and cancellation never propagates.
bugs.evidence: Lines 140-142: `suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): Result<User> = runCatching { api.getUser(id).toDomain() }`. runCatching { } catches CancellationException in a suspend context, silently defeating structured-concurrency cancellation; the recommended approach is a try/catch that rethrows CancellationException or a coroutine-aware Result helper.

bugs.description: The side-effects Channel is collected in a plain LaunchedEffect(Unit) with no repeatOnLifecycle, so effects (navigation, snackbar) are consumed while the screen is backgrounded, causing off-screen navigation and lost/mis-timed UI effects.
bugs.evidence: Lines 119-128: `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.sideEffects.collect { effect -> when (effect) { is HomeSideEffect.NavigateToDetail -> onNavigateToDetail(effect.itemId) ... } } }`. The collector stays active while STOPPED, so a NavigateToDetail emitted off-screen fires immediately on top of another destination. The buffered Channel only behaves correctly if collection pauses when backgrounded (repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)), as rcosteira android-dev/SKILL.md:90-99 shows.

bugs.description: Initial load is dispatched from LaunchedEffect(Unit) inside the composable, so it re-fires whenever the activity/composition is recreated (e.g. on configuration change), reloading data on every rotation and discarding progress.
bugs.evidence: Lines 131-133: `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.onIntent(HomeIntent.LoadItems) }`. Unlike a ViewModel init{} block (which runs once and survives config changes), LaunchedEffect(Unit) re-runs on recomposition-from-recreation, so rotation triggers a redundant LoadItems. Either move the trigger into the ViewModel or guard it with rememberSaveable.

contradictions.topic: kotlinx.serialization encodeDefaults flag for the Ktor client Json config
contradictions.claimA: Always set encodeDefaults = true for client APIs. With the default (false), any property equal to its declared default is stripped from the payload, so protocol-constant fields like jsonrpc="2.0" or version="1.0" silently vanish and the server rejects the request.
contradictions.claimB: Configures the shared ContentNegotiation Json with encodeDefaults = false in the KMP HttpClientFactory, which is exactly the setting rcosteira warns causes protocol-constant fields to disappear.
contradictions.evidence: rcosteira kmp-ktor SKILL.md line 15 (`Json { ... encodeDefaults = true }`) and line 34 ("Always set it for client APIs"), vs ahmed kmp-networking SKILL.md line 58 (`encodeDefaults = false`). ahmed ktor-patterns also omits the flag (defaults to false) at lines 16-20. These are opposing recommendations for the same Ktor+kotlinx.serialization client config.

contradictions.topic: Which exception type to catch when wrapping network calls at the boundary
contradictions.claimA: Catch SPECIFIC Ktor types (ClientRequestException / ServerResponseException / HttpRequestTimeoutException / IOException) and map to DataError; explicitly warns that `catch (e: Exception)` would swallow CancellationException.
contradictions.claimB: The canonical `apiCall` wrapper catches generic `Exception` and maps everything (including CancellationException) to a NetworkException; the ktor-patterns `safeRequest` uses `runCatching` which catches all Throwable.
contradictions.evidence: rcosteira kmp-ktor SKILL.md line 89 ("`catch (e: Exception)` would swallow CancellationException") vs ahmed kmp-networking SKILL.md lines 311-315 (`catch (e: Exception) { ApiResult.Error(e.toNetworkException()) }`) and ahmed ktor-patterns SKILL.md lines 99-112 (`runCatching { ... }`). Directly opposing guidance on the same coroutine-boundary catch.

bugs.description: The `apiCall` wrapper catches generic `Exception`, which includes kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException. It routes cancellation through `toNetworkException()` (line 264 else-branch -> NetworkException) and returns it as ApiResult.Error, swallowing the cancellation and breaking structured concurrency.
bugs.evidence: Lines 311-315: `catch (e: Exception) { ApiResult.Error(e.toNetworkException()) }`; toNetworkException (lines 264-279) maps any unknown Throwable to `NetworkException(...)`, so a cancelled coroutine is silently converted to an error result instead of propagating.

bugs.description: `safeRequest` uses `runCatching`, which catches all Throwable (including CancellationException). This swallows coroutine cancellation the same way, and is presented as the recommended safe-request helper.
bugs.evidence: Lines 99-112: `suspend inline fun <reified T> HttpClient.safeRequest(...): Result<T> = runCatching { ... }`. runCatching catches Throwable, so CancellationException is captured into Result.failure instead of rethrown.

bugs.description: The bearer `refreshTokens` block calls `client.post("auth/refresh")` on the same authenticated client without `markAsRefreshTokenRequest()`. When a refresh itself returns 401, the Auth plugin intercepts the refresh request and triggers another refresh, causing an infinite refresh loop (the exact pitfall rcosteira documents).
bugs.evidence: Lines 48-54: `refreshTokens { val response = client.post("auth/refresh") { setBody(...) } ... }` — no `markAsRefreshTokenRequest()`. Contrast rcosteira kmp-ktor SKILL.md line 42 and 51 which mark the refresh call to skip the Auth plugin.

bugs.description: The `OfflineCapableApi` example will not compile. (1) It declares `class OfflineCapableApi<T : Any>(...) : OfflineCapableApi<T> by api` — a class cannot delegate to itself, and `by api` requires an interface that `api: T` implements. (2) It calls `ttl.toMillisMilliseconds()`, which is not a kotlin.time.Duration function (real API: `inWholeMilliseconds`). (3) It compares `Long + Long > Clock.System.now()`, i.e. a Long against an Instant, which is a type error.
bugs.evidence: Lines 357-360 (self-delegating class header), line 369 (`cached.timestamp + ttl.toMillisMilliseconds() > Clock.System.now()`).

contradictions.topic: How to scope Activity-lifetime dependencies that must survive configuration changes (the common case)
contradictions.claimA: Scope Activity-bound dependencies with a plain instance scope: `scope<MainActivity> { scoped { NavigationController() } }`, accessed via `KoinScopeComponent` + `activityScope()`. Presented as THE 'Activity scope' pattern with no config-change caveat.
contradictions.claimB: For the common case that must survive configuration changes, use `activityRetainedScope` (backed by the Activity's retained ViewModel) accessed via `AndroidScopeComponent`, and reserve a plain `scope<T>` only for a 'Custom lifetime not tied to an Activity.' Explicitly: 'do not hand-roll createScope / close for this case.'
contradictions.evidence: ahmed: /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/everything-claude-code-mobile/skills/koin-patterns/SKILL.md lines 99-112 — `scope<MainActivity> { scoped { NavigationController() } }` and `override val scope: Scope by activityScope()` under a heading simply titled 'Scopes / Activity scope'. rcosteira: /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/android-skills/plugins/android-skills/skills/koin/SKILL.md lines 46-62 — 'Survives configuration changes (the common case) -> activityRetainedScope ... backed by the Activity's retained ViewModel, so it lives across rotation'; the plain `scope<T>` is scoped to 'Custom lifetime not tied to an Activity.' The two skills recommend opposing APIs (`activityScope`/`KoinScopeComponent` vs `activityRetainedScope`/`AndroidScopeComponent`) for the same decision, and would give an agent conflicting guidance when both auto-trigger on `scoped { }`.

bugs.description: The 'Activity scope' pattern loses state across configuration changes. A `scope<MainActivity>` obtained via `activityScope()` is bound to the Activity instance lifecycle; on rotation the Activity is destroyed and recreated, the scope is closed, and `scoped { NavigationController() }` is re-created, silently discarding any state it held. For state that should survive config changes this is the wrong API (rcosteira uses `activityRetainedScope` precisely to fix this).
bugs.evidence: Lines 99-112: `scope<MainActivity> { scoped { NavigationController() } }` with `class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity(), KoinScopeComponent { override val scope: Scope by activityScope() }`. No caveat that this scope dies on rotation; contrast rcosteira SKILL.md lines 46-52 which mandates `activityRetainedScope` for the config-change-surviving common case.

bugs.description: `single { android.content.Context() }` does not compile / is technically impossible: android.content.Context is an abstract class with no public constructor, so it cannot be instantiated. The Android Context must be supplied to Koin via `androidContext(this@MyApp)` in `startKoin` and resolved with `androidContext()` / `get()` — which ahmed's own koin-patterns file does correctly (line 59).
bugs.evidence: Line 61 inside `androidPlatformModule`: `single { android.content.Context() }`. Compare koin-patterns/SKILL.md line 59 `androidContext(this@MyApp)` and rcosteira SKILL.md line 8 `androidContext(this@MyApp)` which is the correct provisioning mechanism.

bugs.description: `single<UserService>(override = true) { ... }` uses the definition-level `override` parameter, which was deprecated in Koin 3.2 (overriding became implicit/last-wins by default) and removed in Koin 4.x. Against a current `koin-bom` (as rcosteira assumes) this fails to compile; the modern approach is to simply declare the fake last, or use module-level override configuration.
bugs.evidence: Lines 224-226: `single<UserService>(override = true) { get<MockUserService>() }`. rcosteira SKILL.md line 8 pins deps 'via koin-bom' (current Koin), where the named `override` parameter no longer exists.

bugs.description: `koin-test` is declared as a production `implementation` dependency in the `commonMain` source set instead of `commonTest`. This ships the Koin test library in the shipped artifact and pollutes main-source API surface; it should be `implementation` under `commonTest` (or a test-only source set).
bugs.evidence: Lines 14-21: inside `val commonMain by getting { dependencies { ... implementation("io.insert-koin:koin-test:${koinVersion}") } }`.

bugs.description: The Service Locator's `get` does an unchecked generic cast and has no fail-fast for a missing key: `services[key] as T`. A missing key yields `null`, and because of type erasure the cast does not throw at the call site, so the null propagates and NPEs somewhere unrelated later. There is no error for an unregistered service and the API is not type-safe.
bugs.evidence: Lines 183-186: `fun <T> get(key: String): T { return services[key] as T }` inside `object ServiceLocator`, with no null/missing-key handling.

bugs.description: The Qualifiers 'Usage' example implies constructor-level `@Named` auto-injection while everything else in the file uses the Classic DSL. With the Classic DSL a `@Named("auth")` annotation on a constructor parameter is inert — Koin resolves constructor args from the definition lambda, so named deps must be resolved with `get(named("auth"))` in the module. `@Named` on the constructor only takes effect with koin-annotations (KSP), which this file never sets up.
bugs.evidence: Lines 117-126: declaration `single(named("auth")) { createAuthClient() }` (Classic DSL) followed by usage `class UserApi(@Named("auth") private val client: HttpClient)`. No `get(named("auth"))` wiring and no koin-annotations processor is shown, so the annotation has no effect.

contradictions.topic: Catching exceptions in coroutine/Flow data-layer code (CancellationException handling)
contradictions.claimA: A `.catch`/try-catch in a coroutine Flow must match IOException specifically and rethrow everything else; a broad catch is explicitly forbidden because it swallows CancellationException and breaks structured concurrency. Correct form: `.catch { e -> if (e is IOException) emit(emptyPreferences()) else throw e }`.
contradictions.claimB: Repeatedly wraps suspend/Flow work in a broad `catch (e: Exception)` with no CancellationException rethrow, exactly the anti-pattern rcosteira forbids (e.g. networkBoundResource `catch (e: Exception) { onFetchFailed(e) }`).

A bare `catch { emit(emptyPreferences()) }` swallows `CancellationException` (breaking structured concurrency)". CONTRA ahmed offline-first/SKILL.md lines 29-31, 84-88, 98-109, 221-227, 277-280 all use broad `catch (e: Exception)` inside flow{}/suspend code. (Note: ahmed's own kmp-repositories/SKILL.md lines 79 & 92 DO rethrow CancellationException correctly, so offline-first is internally inconsistent with ahmed's other skill too.)

contradictions.topic: Where the Result / error boundary sits when a use-case (domain) layer exists
contradictions.claimA: When use cases are present, the REPOSITORY should throw DataError (not return Result), and the USE CASE is the Result boundary that catches it and returns Result<T>; use cases never catch platform exceptions. Repository returns Result directly only when there is NO domain layer.

bugs.description: Broad `catch (e: Exception)` inside flow{}/suspend blocks swallows CancellationException, breaking structured concurrency: on collector cancellation the exception is caught and either ignored (onFetchFailed default = {}) or converted to an emission instead of propagating.
bugs.evidence: networkBoundResource lines 29-31 `catch (e: Exception) { onFetchFailed(e) }` (default onFetchFailed = {} at line 18); getCacheFirst lines 84-88; getNetworkFirst lines 98-109; SyncQueue.processQueue lines 221-227 (also deletes the pending op on max retries). None rethrow CancellationException. This is the exact anti-pattern rcosteira/datastore lines 22-29 warns against.

bugs.description: retryWithBackoff catches Exception (which includes CancellationException) and retries with delay(), treating a cancelled coroutine as a retryable failure. A retry helper must rethrow CancellationException before retrying.
bugs.evidence: Lines 266-283: `repeat(maxRetries - 1) { try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { delay(currentDelay); ... } }`. If block() is cancelled the CancellationException is caught and the loop attempts another delay/retry rather than propagating cancellation (only accidentally rescued by delay()'s own cancellation check).

bugs.description: SyncQueue.enqueue calls `connectivityMonitor.isCurrentlyConnected()`, a method that does not exist on the ConnectivityMonitor interface (which only exposes `isConnected: Flow<Boolean>`). Undefined symbol - will not compile.

bugs.description: The UserLocalDataSource example conflates Room and SQLDelight on the same AppDatabase type and will not compile. The iOS actual also instantiates the abstract @Database class directly via `AppDatabase("$dbPath/app.db")`, which is invalid for Room.

bugs.description: The @Database sets `exportSchema = true` but the skill never configures a schema output directory (no `room { schemaDirectory(...) }` block nor `room.schemaLocation` KSP arg). bugs.description: Uses `@Insert(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE)` named `upsert` and recommends REPLACE for upsert semantics. INSERT OR REPLACE deletes and re-inserts the conflicting row (new rowid, can fire ON DELETE CASCADE on child tables), so it is not a true upsert; Room's dedicated `@Upsert` (since 2.5) is the correct primitive for update-or-insert.
bugs.evidence: Lines 99-100 `@Insert(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE) suspend fun upsert(user: UserEntity): Long`; best-practice line 288 `Prefer OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE for upsert patterns`.

result.depthComparison: Depth splits by axis. By raw volume and copy-paste readiness, ahmed dominates: five skills covering Room (entities, @Embedded, @Relation, TypeConverters, migrations, Koin DI, Flow integration, in-memory DAO testing), KMP repositories (base-repository cache/network/refresh helpers, data sources, use cases, MockK tests), offline-first (NetworkBoundResource, sync queue, conflict resolution, WorkManager + iOS BGTaskScheduler), SQLDelight, and shared serialization models. For breadth of the data-layer surface, ahmed is by far the most detailed. However, by correctness-per-line and modern accuracy, rcosteira is stronger and more actionable in its niche: android-data-layer is terse but is the only source that articulates the layered error-propagation model (repository as error boundary, sealed DataError, Result placement with vs without a domain layer) and the current KMP-Room recipe (@ConstructedBy / RoomDatabaseConstructor / BundledSQLiteDriver / per-target KSP / schema dir); datastore is precise and correctness-first (IOException-specific catch, CorruptionException + ReplaceFileCorruptionHandler, KMP per-platform paths, no runBlocking in Composables). Net: ahmed is the most comprehensive but carries the real bugs (swallowed CancellationException throughout offline-first, a Room/SQLDelight conflation that will not compile, Dispatchers.IO in commonMain); rcosteira is thinner but the guidance it gives is the correct, current guidance and it owns two topics (the error model and DataStore) that ahmed never touches. For a merged plugin, rcosteira should be the authority on error propagation, KMP-Room setup, and DataStore, while ahmed supplies the breadth (SQLDelight, offline/sync, serialization, Room reference detail) after the CancellationException handling is fixed.

contradictions.topic: Primitive for one-shot UI events (navigation / snackbars)
contradictions.claimA: Use a plain MutableSharedFlow (default: no replay, no buffer) for events, exposed as SharedFlow: `private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<Event>(); val events: SharedFlow<Event> = _events.asSharedFlow()`.
contradictions.claimB: A default MutableSharedFlow for nav/snackbar events is a BUG: 'If nothing is collecting at the exact instant of emission, the event is gone.' Use `Channel(BUFFERED).receiveAsFlow()` for single-consumer exactly-once events.
contradictions.evidence: ahmed coroutines-patterns/SKILL.md lines 63-65 (`private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<Event>()`) vs chris kotlin-flow-state-event-modeling/SKILL.md lines 27-37 (marks the identical MutableSharedFlow pattern `// BAD`, recommends `Channel(BUFFERED).receiveAsFlow()` `// GOOD`). rcosteira kotlin-flows/SKILL.md lines 16 & 22 independently agrees with chris: 'SharedFlow(replay = 0) drops the emission if no collector is active,' Channel(BUFFERED).receiveAsFlow() is 'Keep - correct.'

contradictions.topic: Catching broad Exception around a suspend call in a coroutine
contradictions.claimA: Recommended ViewModel error handling wraps a suspend call in a broad catch with no CancellationException rethrow: `try { val result = repository.fetchData(); _state.value = Success(result) } catch (e: Exception) { _state.value = Error(e.message) }`.
contradictions.claimB: 'Catch specific types (IOException, HttpException), never Exception / Throwable' and 'Never catch CancellationException without rethrowing it' — a broad catch swallows CancellationException and breaks structured cancellation.
contradictions.evidence: ahmed coroutines-patterns/SKILL.md lines 90-97 vs rcosteira kotlin-coroutines/SKILL.md lines 57 & 60 (chris kotlin-coroutines-structured-concurrency/SKILL.md §6 lines 281-289 agrees, calling `catch (e: Exception)` around a suspend call 'BAD - catches CancellationException, never rethrows'). Note: ahmed is internally inconsistent — lines 117-125 of the same file DO show the correct `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }` guard, but the primary error-handling example (the one most likely copied) omits it.

contradictions.topic: Manufacturing/owning a CoroutineScope in a helper factory, and using CoroutineExceptionHandler as the remedy
contradictions.claimA: Provides `useCaseScope()` as a reusable pattern that manufactures a fresh `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + PlatformDispatchers.io + CoroutineExceptionHandler { ... })` on every call, and builds ApplicationScope/ViewScope around stored scopes whose safety rests on an attached CoroutineExceptionHandler.
contradictions.claimB: A `CoroutineScope(...)` instantiated inside a function body 'is just a stored scope with extra steps. Each call leaks a new uncancellable scope ... the scope shouldn't exist at all.' And in the review red-flags table: 'I'll just add a CoroutineExceptionHandler to the scope' -> 'The problem isn't error handling. The problem is the scope shouldn't exist.'
contradictions.evidence: ahmed shared-coroutines/SKILL.md lines 122-129 (useCaseScope factory) and 94-106/109-119 (ApplicationScope/ViewScope + CoroutineExceptionHandler) vs chris kotlin-coroutines-structured-concurrency/SKILL.md line 145 and red-flags table line 430.

contradictions.topic: Using withTimeout for network-call timeouts
contradictions.claimA: Provides a standard `networkCall` wrapper built on withTimeout: `protected suspend fun <T> networkCall(timeout: Duration = 30.seconds, block: suspend () -> T): T = withTimeout(timeout) { withContext(PlatformDispatchers.io) { block() } }`.
contradictions.claimB: 'Don't reach for withTimeout for network timeouts — OkHttp/Retrofit/Ktor own those.'
contradictions.evidence: ahmed shared-coroutines/SKILL.md lines 249-256 vs rcosteira kotlin-coroutines/SKILL.md line 49.

bugs.description: The primary ViewModel error-handling example catches broad Exception around the suspend call repository.fetchData() without rethrowing CancellationException. When viewModelScope is cancelled (ViewModel cleared), the cancellation is swallowed and the coroutine sets UiState to Error instead of cancelling, breaking structured concurrency.
bugs.evidence: Lines 90-97: `viewModelScope.launch { try { val result = repository.fetchData(); _state.value = Success(result) } catch (e: Exception) { _state.value = Error(e.message) } }`. The file's own Cancellation section (lines 117-125) shows the correct `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }`, so this example contradicts the file's own guidance.

bugs.description: BackgroundWorker's periodic loop catches broad Exception around work() inside `while (isActive)`, swallowing the CancellationException thrown on cancellation and logging it as a 'failed' worker before delay eventually propagates the cancel. Exactly the swallowed-cancellation anti-pattern the other two sources forbid.
bugs.evidence: Lines 365-374: `workers[key] = scope.launch(dispatcher) { while (isActive) { try { work() } catch (e: Exception) { println("Worker $key failed: $e") }; delay(interval) } }`.

bugs.description: Flow<T>.cachedIn(scope) delegates to a free function `cached(scope)` that does not exist in kotlinx.coroutines (AndroidX Paging exposes cachedIn, not cached). References an undefined symbol — will not compile.
bugs.evidence: Lines 147-149: `fun <T> Flow<T>.cachedIn(scope: CoroutineScope): Flow<T> = cached(scope)`.

bugs.description: The custom StateFlow<T>.shareIn extension ignores all its parameters (scope, started, replay) and just returns the receiver unchanged — a misleading no-op that also shadows the real kotlinx.coroutines shareIn operator. Callers believe they configured replay/started behaviour but get the original flow untouched.
bugs.evidence: Lines 138-144: `fun <T> StateFlow<T>.shareIn(scope, started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000), replay = 1): StateFlow<T> { return this }`.

bugs.description: collectWhileActive leaks: the lifecycle.subscribe { } observer is never removed and there is no ON_DESTROY branch to cancel the returned SupervisorJob, so the created scope/collector outlive the lifecycle; repeated ON_RESUME also stacks new collect calls. (Also depends on a non-standard `Lifecycle.subscribe` API rather than the standard addObserver.)
bugs.evidence: Lines 156-181, esp. the never-unsubscribed `lifecycle.subscribe { event -> ... }` and the missing ON_DESTROY handling; only ON_RESUME/ON_PAUSE are handled and the returned `job` is never cancelled by the helper.

bugs.description: repeatOnViewActive is functionally broken as a 'repeat on view active' operator: if isActive() is false at first evaluation the while-loop never runs and the flow completes immediately (never resumes when the view later becomes active); two coroutines (the collector and the loop) call send concurrently and the loop re-emits the cached lastValue every interval, producing duplicate/stale emissions; and the T? null sentinel silently drops legitimate nulls for nullable T.
bugs.evidence: Lines 184-204: `channelFlow { var lastValue: T? = null; val collectorJob = launch { collect { value -> lastValue = value; if (isActive()) send(value) } }; while (isActive()) { lastValue?.let { send(it) }; delay(minInterval) }; collectorJob.cancel() }`.

result.depthComparison: chris is the most detailed and actionable source for this cluster. Its kotlin-coroutines-structured-concurrency skill (~440 lines) is a review-oriented playbook: seven numbered anti-patterns each with BAD/GOOD fixes, the silent-cancellation mechanism explained, a DI-singleton/Initializer-that-launches section with three ranked refactor patterns, a ContentProvider runBlocking carve-out, a quick-reference symptom->fix table, leaf-first refactoring steps, and 'thought vs reality' red-flag tables. Its kotlin-flow-state-event-modeling skill is similarly deep on state/event primitive selection. rcosteira is a very close second and is the most technically accurate and modern: it is tight but high-signal, deliberately skips basics, and uniquely nails concrete Flow operator traps (callbackFlow awaitClose, retryWhen attempt guard, combine waits-for-all, Kotlin 2.4 backing fields, tryEmit drop semantics) plus a correct suspendRunCatching. ahmed is the shallowest on principled guidance: coroutines-patterns is an introductory cheat-sheet, and shared-coroutines is a large KMP code library (dispatchers, base classes, worker, test helpers) that is copy-paste scaffolding rather than reasoning. Notably, every bug found in this audit is in ahmed's two files; chris's and rcosteira's code examples were technically correct. For a merged plugin, chris/rcosteira should own the coroutines+flow guidance; ahmed's value is narrowly the KMP scaffolding, which needs the bug fixes above first.

uniqueValue.whatIsUnique: Only source with concrete KMP scaffolding: an expect/actual PlatformDispatcher abstraction including real iOS GCD-backed dispatchers (NSQueueDispatcher / DispatchQueueDispatcher over dispatch_get_main_queue / global queues), the build.gradle.kts sourceSets dependency setup for kotlinx-coroutines in commonMain/androidMain, reusable BaseRepository / BaseUseCase / BaseNoParamsUseCase / FlowUseCase base classes that wrap results in Result and (correctly, unlike its other examples) rethrow CancellationException, a keyed BackgroundWorker periodic-task manager, and a TestPlatformDispatcher for tests. Worth keeping for KMP once the noted defects are fixed.

kotlin-coroutines-structured-concurrency uniquely covers: the DI-bound singleton / Initializer.initialize()-that-launches anti-pattern (§5) with three ranked refactor patterns (invert into the consumer / WorkManager scheduled work / explicit named launch site), the distinction that Initializers are fine only if they register not launch, the android.content.ContentProvider runBlocking carve-out, runBlocking-in-tests -> runTest, leaf-first incremental refactoring guidance, and 'thought vs reality' review red-flag tables.

kotlin-flow-state-event-modeling uniquely covers: phasing to avoid fake-domain sentinel initial values (don't expose the StateFlow until the real value exists), the `stateIn()`-called-inside-a-function anti-pattern (a new never-completing sharing coroutine per call), `.map` on a StateFlow silently losing `.value` (terminate with `.stateIn`), and MutableStateFlow.update{} atomicity with the rule to build expensive objects outside the update lambda because it can retry.

kotlin-flows uniquely covers: callback bridging (suspendCancellableCoroutine vs suspendCoroutine, callbackFlow with mandatory awaitClose to avoid leaks), retry/retryWhen with a mandatory attempt-count guard to avoid infinite retry, the `combine` waits-for-every-input-to-emit 'stuck on Loading' trap (and that destructuring in combine doesn't compile), the Kotlin 2.4 explicit backing-field (`field =`) idiom, BroadcastChannel/ConflatedBroadcastChannel migration table, tryEmit-silently-drops vs launch{emit}, and moving side effects out of combine/map into onEach.

kotlin-coroutines uniquely states the main-safety rule (the function doing blocking work owns withContext(io); callers never switch dispatchers), provides a correct reusable suspendRunCatching that rethrows CancellationException, warns that viewModelScope already uses SupervisorJob (don't add another), flags MainScope() as unstructured like GlobalScope, warns against withTimeout for network timeouts, and gives KMP dispatcher/scope injection guidance including expect/actual Dispatchers.Main.immediate.

contradictions.topic: Test doubles for substituting collaborators: mocks vs fakes
contradictions.claimA: Isolate collaborators with Mockk mocks. ViewModel tests declare `@MockK private lateinit var repository` and stub with `coEvery { repository.getItems() } returns ...`; repository tests mock the API the same way (`@MockK ... api`, `coEvery { api.getUser("1") } returns UserDto(...)`). Mock-based isolation is the demonstrated default across the entire skill.
contradictions.claimB: Prefer fakes over mocks. android-testing/SKILL.md line 13 names "fakes over mocks" as an established foundational principle the skill builds on; chris aligns with this — compose-ui-testing-patterns/SKILL.md line 160 lists "Testing click behavior through a ViewModel mock" as a mistake whose fix is "Pass a callback and assert it was invoked."
contradictions.evidence: ahmed: mobile-testing/SKILL.md lines 30-31 (`@MockK private lateinit var repository: HomeRepository`) and lines 55-61 (`@MockK private lateinit var api: UserApi` / `coEvery { api.getUser("1") } returns UserDto("1", "John")`). rcosteira: android-testing/SKILL.md line 13 ("...not the basics of the three tiers, fakes over mocks, runTest..."). chris: compose-ui-testing-patterns/SKILL.md lines 160-161 (mistake table).

contradictions.topic: Strictness of test-first (must a failing test always precede production code?)
contradictions.claimA: Strict, no exceptions: "No production code without a failing test first. Write the test, watch it fail (RED)... A behaviour you never watched fail isn't proven." A bug isn't fixed until a test that was red because of the bug is green.
contradictions.claimB: Test-first is optional: tests may be written "first (TDD) OR alongside your code" — writing production code before the test is explicitly permitted.
contradictions.evidence: rcosteira: android-testing/SKILL.md lines 17-18. ahmed: ios-testing/SKILL.md line 306 ("Write them first (TDD) or alongside your code, but always maintain them."); note ahmed's mobile-testing/SKILL.md line 97 says "Write tests first" but the iOS skill relaxes it to "or alongside."

bugs.description: The interaction-state example launches the `interactionSource.emit(...)` on a fresh, detached `TestScope()` that is never advanced, so the coroutine body never executes and the interaction is never emitted — the example does not do what it claims. `TestScope()` uses a StandardTestDispatcher whose scheduler only runs tasks when explicitly pumped (runCurrent/advanceUntilIdle); the following `composeTestRule.waitForIdle()` synchronizes Compose's own work, not this unrelated TestScope. The subsequent 'assert the visual/semantic change that hover produces' therefore asserts against the un-hovered state. Ironically the skill correctly warns not to use `LaunchedEffect` but substitutes an equally non-working driver.
bugs.evidence: Lines 97-105: `TestScope().launch { interactionSource.emit(HoverInteraction.Enter()) }` followed by `composeTestRule.waitForIdle()` with no scheduler advancement. Correct approaches would emit from the test's own coroutine (e.g. within `runTest`/`runComposeUiTest` and advance) or via `composeTestRule` clock, not a detached TestScope.

bugs.description: The ViewModel test constructs `HomeViewModel(repository)` and drives it with `runTest {}` but installs no MainDispatcherRule / `Dispatchers.setMain(...)`. A standard Android ViewModel launches work in `viewModelScope`, which is bound to `Dispatchers.Main`; without replacing Main in a JVM unit test the test throws `IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize`. This is exactly the setup rcosteira's android-testing skill warns about (the two-schedulers trap), and it is absent here.
bugs.evidence: Lines 29-49: `@BeforeEach setup(){ ...; viewModel = HomeViewModel(repository) }` and `fun \`loads items successfully\`() = runTest { ... viewModel.onIntent(LoadItems) ... }` with no MainDispatcherRule anywhere in the skill. Contrast rcosteira android-testing/SKILL.md line 26 (pass `mainRule.dispatcher` into `runTest`).

bugs.description: The Turbine StateFlow test asserts the loading state as the FIRST emission, but `stateFlow.test {}` replays the current (initial) value first. `onIntent(LoadItems)` is called before the first `awaitItem()`, and the initial state (isLoading almost certainly false) is what the first `awaitItem()` returns, so `awaitItem().isLoading shouldBe true` asserts against the wrong item. Correct pattern is to consume/skip the initial item first, then trigger the action; with StandardTestDispatcher the loading emission may also be conflated away without an explicit advance.
bugs.evidence: Lines 43-47: `viewModel.state.test { viewModel.onIntent(LoadItems); awaitItem().isLoading shouldBe true; awaitItem().items shouldBe listOf(item) }` — no initial `awaitItem()`/`skipItems(1)` before triggering the intent.

bugs.description: The Espresso flaky-fix snippet uses `@IdlingResource` as an annotation on a property, but there is no such annotation — `androidx.test.espresso.IdlingResource` is an interface. The snippet will not compile and teaches a nonexistent API; a `CountingIdlingResource` is used by registering it via `IdlingRegistry.getInstance().register(...)`, not by annotating a field. `@get:Rule val disableAnimationsRule = DisableAnimationsRule()` also references a non-standard/undefined class.
bugs.evidence: Lines 116-124: `@IdlingResource val countingIdlingResource = CountingIdlingResource("api")` and `@get:Rule val disableAnimationsRule = DisableAnimationsRule()`.

bugs.description: Presents wrapping content in `CompositionLocalProvider(LocalInspectionMode provides true)` as the fix strategy for Compose test flakiness whose listed causes are 'Recomposition timing / State hoisting issues / Animation interference.' `LocalInspectionMode` is a preview/inspection flag; it does not control recomposition timing, state hoisting, or the test clock, so it is not a remedy for those flake causes. The correct levers (per rcosteira) are `mainClock.autoAdvance=false` before setContent, `advanceTimeByFrame()`, and `mainClock.advanceTimeUntil { ... }`.
bugs.evidence: Lines 135-150: under 'Compose Tests ... Common Flaky Causes: Recomposition timing / State hoisting issues / Animation interference', the 'Fix Strategies' block is `CompositionLocalProvider(LocalInspectionMode provides true){ content() }`.

contradictionVerdicts.topic: Which load state to gate the full-screen (initial) loader on
contradictionVerdicts.reasoning: Both quotes are accurate. ahmed SKILL.md lines 169-172 gate the full-screen loader on the combined `articles.loadState.refresh` (when(articles.loadState.refresh){ is LoadState.Loading -> CircularProgressIndicator }). rcosteira SKILL.md line 55 explicitly says '**not** the combined loadState.refresh', instead gate on `loadState.source.refresh` + `itemCount == 0`, giving the RemoteMediator/Room timing rationale. On the literal surface they oppose. But this is NOT a clean same-scenario contradiction: rcosteira's rule lives in its '## RemoteMediator (offline-first)' section and its stated reason ('flips to NotLoading before Room finishes writing') is specific to a RemoteMediator + Room-backed PagingSource, where mediator and source refresh states differ. ahmed's PaginatedList composable operates on LazyPagingItems<Article> (the network-only PagingSource path, lines 22-53/86-100) where there is no RemoteMediator, so loadState.refresh == loadState.source.refresh and ahmed's gating is actually correct; ahmed additionally guards itemCount==0 in the NotLoading branch (line 181). ahmed never applies his UI load-state pattern to his own RemoteMediator/ArticleEntity flow (lines 200-259 have no Compose UI, and the types differ: Article vs ArticleEntity). The genuine conflict only materializes if an agent, with both skills merged, applies ahmed's generic loader pattern to offline-first paging — which is a real risk but a context-conditional one, not a universal head-to-head contradiction. Hence PARTIAL: real opposing wording on the same API, reconcilable by context, dangerous only in the overlapping offline-first case.

bugVerdicts.description: CursorArticlePagingSource.load() catches broad `Exception` and returns LoadResult.Error(e), swallowing kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified at ahmed SKILL.md lines 74-76: `} catch (e: Exception) { LoadResult.Error(e) }`. CancellationException (java.util.concurrent.CancellationException) is a subclass of Exception, so this catch swallows it and converts a cancelled load into a paging Error state instead of letting it propagate. This is a well-established anti-pattern for coroutines/structured concurrency. Paging can cancel an in-flight load (invalidation while a load is in progress, fast scroll cancelling a prefetch), and a swallowed cancellation surfaces as a spurious Error -> retry UI. The contrast the finding cites is correct: ahmed's own ArticlePagingSource at lines 40-44 catches only IOException and HttpException (the officially recommended pattern that lets CancellationException through). The cursor source deviates from that same-file correct pattern. Real bug; 'major' is slightly high (practical impact is often a transient/rarely-observed error state) but the defect is genuine.

bugVerdicts.description: ArticleRemoteMediator.load() catches broad `Exception` and returns MediatorResult.Error(e), swallowing CancellationException.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified at ahmed SKILL.md lines 245-247: `} catch (e: Exception) { MediatorResult.Error(e) }`. Same mechanism as bug 1 — CancellationException is caught and turned into MediatorResult.Error, breaking cooperative cancellation and surfacing via loadState.mediator as a spurious error. The recommended pattern (and ahmed's own PagingSource at lines 40-44) catches specific IOException/HttpException. Real defect. Note: broad `catch (e: Exception)` in RemoteMediator is fairly common in tutorials, so severity is arguably medium, but the CancellationException-swallowing concern is valid and matters.

bugVerdicts.description: PaginatedList renders the list TWICE inside the same Box: once in the loadState.refresh==NotLoading branch and again inside PullToRefreshBox.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified at ahmed SKILL.md lines 167-197. The `when (articles.loadState.refresh)` block and the `PullToRefreshBox` are both direct children of the same `Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize())`. In the NotLoading + itemCount>0 case, line 184 calls `ArticleLazyColumn(articles = articles)`, and lines 190-196 render `ArticleLazyColumn(articles = articles)` a second time inside PullToRefreshBox. Box stacks children on the z-axis, so two full-size LazyColumns overlap. Worse, in the Loading branch the CircularProgressIndicator (line 171) shows while the PullToRefreshBox still composes an (empty) list beneath it, and in the Error branch ErrorScreen overlaps the list; the empty/error states are visually stacked with the list. The isRefreshing at line 191 (`loadState.refresh is LoadState.Loading`) also double-fires with the when's Loading branch. Clearly broken structure — the pull-to-refresh should wrap a single list, not duplicate it. Real bug, 'major' is appropriate.

bugVerdicts.description: RemoteMediator LoadType.REFRESH network call uses state.config.pageSize instead of state.config.initialLoadSize for the first page.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified at ahmed SKILL.md line 228: `api.getArticles(page = page, pageSize = state.config.pageSize)`, and the offline Pager at line 255 uses `PagingConfig(pageSize = 20)` with no initialLoadSize override, so initialLoadSize defaults to 3*pageSize = 60. Google's RemoteMediator guidance uses `state.config.initialLoadSize` for the REFRESH load so the first fetch fills the initial window; using pageSize under-fetches (writes 20 rows while the Room PagingSource's initial load requests 60). This is a legitimate deviation from recommended practice. One caveat on the finding's wording: it does not necessarily trigger an 'immediate' extra APPEND — the extra network round-trip fires when the user scrolls within prefetchDistance of the (short) loaded set, which for 20 items on a typical screen may be near-immediate but is not guaranteed on first frame. Core claim correct; 'minor' severity is right.

bugVerdicts.description: enablePlaceholders=false but the item body handles the null (placeholder) case and Best Practices advises shimmer placeholders; the null-branch is dead code and advice mismatches config.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Two sub-claims, verified separately. (1) Dead-branch: correct. enablePlaceholders=false at line 93; itemCount then equals the loaded-item count, so `articles[index]` for index in [0,itemCount) returns non-null, and the `else -> ArticlePlaceholder()` branch (lines 141-143) is effectively unreachable in normal operation. This is accurate, but it is a benign, defensive null-check (the official Compose Paging examples themselves write `pagingItems[i]?.let{}` as a safety net), not a functional defect — nothing renders wrong. (2) Advice-vs-config mismatch: weak. 'Show shimmer placeholders during initial load' (line 394) most naturally refers to a full-screen skeleton during the refresh Loading state, which is independent of Paging's enablePlaceholders flag (that flag controls greyed rows at not-yet-loaded scroll positions). ahmed in fact shows the initial loader via CircularProgressIndicator, not via the null-branch. So the guidance does not strictly require enablePlaceholders=true, and the claimed contradiction between advice and config is loose. Net: the dead-code observation is technically true but harmless; the 'guidance does not match config' framing overstates it. PARTIAL — real minor inconsistency, not a bug that meaningfully matters.

missedIssues: MISSED (ahmed, likely real, page-keyed initialLoadSize pitfall): ArticlePagingSource sets initialLoadSize=40 with pageSize=20 (lines 91-94) but uses naive page-number keys — the initial REFRESH load requests params.loadSize=40 for page=1 and returns nextKey=page+1=2 (line 38). If the API interprets (page,pageSize) as offset=(page-1)*pageSize (the standard REST semantics implied by the offset-based JSON at lines 356-366), then load 1 = page 1 x 40 = items 1-40, and load 2 = page 2 x 20 = items 21-40, DUPLICATING items 21-40 at the initial-load/second-page boundary. This is the classic Paging-3 foot-gun when initialLoadSize != pageSize with page-based keys; the finding flagged the mirror problem in the RemoteMediator (bug 4) but missed it in the primary PagingSource. API-semantics dependent, but a genuine correctness risk.

bugVerdicts.description: DiskCache.Builder().directory(context.cacheDir.resolve("image_cache")) passes a java.io.File where Coil 3 requires okio.Path; compile error, occurs twice.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified in the file. The two occurrences are at lines 115 (.directory(context.cacheDir.resolve("image_cache"))) and 136 (.directory(androidContext().cacheDir.resolve("image_cache"))) - the finding cited 116/137, off by one, but the code is present. context.cacheDir is a java.io.File and File.resolve(String) is a Kotlin stdlib extension returning File. Coil 3's DiskCache.Builder.directory() takes okio.Path with no File overload (Coil moved to okio for multiplatform; the Coil 2 File signature was dropped). Kotlin performs no implicit File->Path conversion, so this is a genuine type-mismatch compile error against the declared coil3 3.0.4. The finding's supporting point is also accurate: the file DID adopt the Coil 3 MemoryCache API (no-arg MemoryCache.Builder() + maxSizePercent(context, 0.25) at lines 108-109), making the File-based directory call an unconverted Coil 2 signature. CONFIRMED (line numbers 115/136, not 116/137).

bugVerdicts.description: BlurTransformation(LocalContext.current, radius = 25f) is a Coil 2 API removed in Coil 3.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified at line 93 as a commented alternative inside transformations(): '// or BlurTransformation(LocalContext.current, radius = 25f)'. The Context-based BlurTransformation is a Coil 2 API (coil.transform.BlurTransformation, which relied on Android RenderScript). Coil 3 (coil3.transform) ships only CircleCropTransformation and RoundedCornersTransformation in core; the Context/RenderScript-based BlurTransformation was dropped for multiplatform, so the symbol is undefined against coil3 3.0.4. The surrounding CircleCropTransformation() and RoundedCornersTransformation(16f) do exist in Coil 3, confirming this one line is the stale Coil 2 signature. Mitigating factor (correctly noted by the finding, keeps it minor): it is commented out, so it does not break the build as-is - it only fails to compile if a user uncomments the suggested option. Guidance is wrong for the declared version, so CONFIRMED at minor severity.

bugVerdicts.description: ImageLoader.Builder(context).respectCacheHeaders(true) is a Coil 2 method removed from ImageLoader.Builder in Coil 3.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified at line 119, chained on ImageLoader.Builder(context) (block lines 105-120). respectCacheHeaders(Boolean) was an ImageLoader.Builder method in Coil 2. In Coil 3, HTTP handling moved out of the core ImageLoader into the separate network artifacts (coil-network-okhttp / coil-network-ktor), and cache-header behavior is now controlled via CacheStrategy on the network fetcher factory; respectCacheHeaders was removed from ImageLoader.Builder. Calling it on ImageLoader.Builder in coil3 3.0.4 is an undefined method -> compile error. The finding hedged this as 'plausible/version-dependent'; I am confident it is a real removal for Coil 3, so CONFIRMED at minor severity.

bugVerdicts.description: iOS CachedAsyncImage .task catch swallows all errors (including cancellation) with only a '// log error' comment, then unconditionally sets isLoading=false.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified at lines 256-261: do { image = try await ImageCache.shared.image(for: url) } catch { // log error } isLoading = false. The catch is effectively empty - the comment '// log error' does not actually log - so every thrown error, including URLSession/task CancellationError, is silently discarded and isLoading is set false unconditionally, so a cancelled load is treated as a normal (failed) completion. The code observation is factually accurate and matches the flagged silent-error-swallowing anti-pattern. Caveats (as the finding itself states): this is out of scope for the Coil/Android image-loading cluster (it is SwiftUI/iOS code), it is genuinely low severity (a cancelled .task usually means the view disappeared, so the isLoading=false has little visible effect), and it is a code-quality/anti-pattern observation rather than a functional Coil bug. Real but minor and out-of-cluster; CONFIRMED as an accurate finding.

result.depthComparison:
Only two of the three named sources have navigation content in scope: ahmed (three dedicated skills) and rcosteira (a single references/navigation.md inside the compose skill). There is no 'chris' navigation content here, so this cluster is an ahmed-vs-rcosteira comparison.

For raw depth and actionability, AHMED dominates. It ships three code-heavy skills: navigation-compose (type-safe routes, NavHost, args, savedStateHandle result passing, deep links, nested graphs, bottom nav with saveState/restoreState/launchSingleTop, animated transitions, TestNavHostController testing, best practices), kmp-navigation (Voyager/Decompose/platform-native expect-actual bridge, tabs, KMP deep linking, type-safe args, state preservation), and deep-linking (Android App Links + assetlinks.json + keytool, iOS Universal Links + AASA + Associated Domains, Info.plist URL schemes, SceneDelegate/AppDelegate + SwiftUI onOpenURL, deferred links, adb/simctl test commands, analytics). Nobody else comes close on breadth or copy-pasteable volume. The caveat is quality: several ahmed snippets are buggy or won't compile (see bugs), and the kmp-navigation file in particular is riddled with non-compiling code.

For correctness and currency, RCOSTEIRA is stronger despite being a fraction of the length. It is the only source that (a) treats Navigation 3 as the default for new work and correctly labels Nav2 as legacy/interop, (b) deliberately delegates Nav3 detail to Google's official navigation-3 skill and the nav3-recipes repo to avoid drift, and (c) supplies high-signal architectural guardrails ahmed lacks entirely (serializable destination keys as fields not captured callbacks, no @Composable lambdas in destination data, ViewModels emitting Flow<NavEvent> collected in a LaunchedEffect rather than holding a NavController, and correct nav-entry decorator nesting order). It is thin on ready-to-paste code but architecturally more correct and forward-looking.

Net: keep ahmed for the concrete Nav2 recipes and the cross-platform deep-linking breadth (after fixing the bugs), and keep rcosteira for Nav3-first direction and the compose-shape guardrails. Where they disagree (Nav2-vs-Nav3 as default; string routes), rcosteira reflects current Android guidance.

contradictionVerdicts.topic: How to collect the one-shot effects/side-effects Channel in Compose (lifecycle scoping)
contradictionVerdicts.reasoning: Verified in the files. ahmed mvi-architecture/SKILL.md lines 120-128 collect the effects flow in a plain `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.sideEffects.collect { ... } }` with NO repeatOnLifecycle. rcosteira android-dev/SKILL.md line 57 explicitly mandates the opposite: 'Collect it in a `LaunchedEffect` (lifecycle-scoped via `repeatOnLifecycle`), never `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`', and the example at lines 90-99 wraps the collect in `lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { viewModel.effects.collect { ... } }`. Both sides use the same source stream — `Channel(Channel.BUFFERED).receiveAsFlow()` (ahmed lines 67-68; rcosteira lines 79-81) — so the only divergence is the collection site, and it is a genuine opposing-pattern conflict. With plain LaunchedEffect the composition stays alive while the Activity is STOPPED, so an effect emitted while backgrounded is consumed immediately (off-screen navigation/snackbar); rcosteira's repeatOnLifecycle cancels collection when STOPPED so the buffered Channel replays on resume. This is the exact behavior rcosteira's rationale depends on, and ahmed's template defeats it. Real conflict on the same decision.

contradictionVerdicts.topic: Where the initial data load is triggered (UI composable vs ViewModel init)
contradictionVerdicts.reasoning: Both sources are ahmed and the code differs exactly as claimed. mvi-architecture/SKILL.md lines 131-133 trigger the load from the UI: `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.onIntent(HomeIntent.LoadItems) }`. android-patterns/SKILL.md lines 107-109 trigger it inside the ViewModel: `init { loadData() }`. These are genuinely different trigger sites for the same 'load the screen's data on first display' decision, and they behave differently across configuration change: `init{}` runs once per (retained) ViewModel and survives rotation, whereas `LaunchedEffect(Unit)` re-runs when the composition is recreated on rotation, re-issuing LoadItems and re-fetching. It is a real within-author divergence (and one that is not purely stylistic, since the init approach avoids the rotation-reload). Note the MVI 'dispatch intent from the UI' idiom is internally consistent with MVI philosophy while init{} is the plain-MVVM idiom, but as concrete emitted code for the same task the two skills conflict.

contradictionVerdicts.topic: Default dependency-injection framework for greenfield ViewModel/Compose code
contradictionVerdicts.reasoning: The code divergence is real: ahmed mvi-architecture line 112 and android-patterns line 127 both use `koinViewModel()`; rcosteira android-dev line 20 names the house default 'DI: Hilt + KSP (or android-skills:koin when the project uses Koin)' and the greenfield example at line 87 uses `hiltViewModel()`. So for a greenfield project the two clusters would emit opposing DI wiring (Koin vs Hilt). However it is a divergent DEFAULT, not an absolute contradiction: (1) rcosteira explicitly permits Koin when the project already uses it, and (2) neither ahmed skill contains any prescriptive DI rule or 'house defaults' section — Koin appears only implicitly in example code, never stated as a mandated default. So claimA ('Both ahmed skills use Koin unconditionally as THE default') is an inference from examples rather than a stated rule. Real greenfield divergence, softened by rcosteira's hedge and the absence of an explicit ahmed prescription — hence PARTIAL.

bugVerdicts.description: retry() declared as plain (non-suspend) fun but calls delay(1000) and invokes a suspend lambda block(); does not compile.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified android-patterns/SKILL.md lines 156-165. `fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: suspend () -> T): T` is NOT marked `suspend`, yet its body calls `block()` (typed `suspend () -> T`) and `delay(1000)` (a suspend function). Both can only be invoked from a coroutine or another suspend function, so the compiler rejects this ('Suspend function should be called only from a coroutine or another suspend function'). The `repeat { }` lambda is inline so its body runs in retry's own non-suspend context — no rescue. Signature must be `suspend fun retry(...)`. It is presented under the recommended 'Higher-Order Functions' section. Genuine, unambiguous compile error. Critical severity is fair.

bugVerdicts.description: retry() catches Exception, swallowing CancellationException and breaking structured concurrency; the loop keeps retrying/delaying after its scope is cancelled.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: The factual half is true: android-patterns lines 160-163 `catch (e: Exception) { delay(1000) }` does catch CancellationException (on JVM it extends Exception), and the idiomatic fix is a preceding `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }` — which the sibling rcosteira skill literally cites at line 140 ('// rethrow first — a broad catch would swallow CancellationException'). But the described FAILURE SCENARIO is inaccurate for this specific code: after the catch, `delay(1000)` executes, and in a cancelled coroutine `delay` is itself a cancellation point that immediately re-throws CancellationException (it does NOT wait 1000ms and does NOT loop). So genuine job-cancellation propagates out of retry via the delay rather than being swallowed into an endless retry loop. The residual real defect is only the missing CancellationException rethrow (a spurious, still-active-scope CancellationException from e.g. a nested withTimeout would be treated as retryable). Real anti-pattern, but the stated consequence ('keeps retrying and delaying after cancellation') does not occur. Also moot in isolation since bug #1 means it never compiles.

bugVerdicts.description: fetchUser() wraps a suspend network call in runCatching, catching CancellationException and converting a cancelled call to Result.failure so cancellation never propagates.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified android-patterns lines 140-142: `suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): Result<User> = runCatching { api.getUser(id).toDomain() }`, marked '✅' at line 139. `runCatching` catches Throwable, including CancellationException. `api.getUser(id)` is a cancellable suspend call; if the coroutine is cancelled during it, the CancellationException is captured into `Result.failure` and the function returns NORMALLY — unlike the retry case there is no subsequent cancellation point (no delay) to re-throw, so cancellation is genuinely swallowed. The caller chain (lines 145-150: `.onFailure { showError(it) }`) would then render an error instead of respecting cancellation, breaking structured concurrency. Well-documented Kotlin anti-pattern; correct form is try/catch that rethrows CancellationException. Major severity fair.

bugVerdicts.description: Side-effects Channel collected in plain LaunchedEffect(Unit) with no repeatOnLifecycle, so effects (navigation, snackbar) fire while the screen is backgrounded.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified mvi-architecture lines 119-128. The collector `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.sideEffects.collect { ... NavigateToDetail/ShowSnackbar/NavigateToLogin ... } }` has no lifecycle gating. The composition stays alive while the Activity is STOPPED, so an effect emitted while backgrounded (e.g. an async result completing after the user backgrounds the app) is delivered immediately: navigation stacks off-screen / a snackbar shows to nobody. The buffered Channel only behaves correctly if collection pauses when backgrounded, which is exactly what rcosteira mandates via repeatOnLifecycle (lines 90-99) and what its buffer-and-replay rationale (line 57) requires. Real, recognized lifecycle defect. It is a subtle correctness/best-practice issue rather than a guaranteed crash, so 'major' is on the strong side but defensible.

bugVerdicts.description: Initial load dispatched from LaunchedEffect(Unit) re-fires on activity/composition recreation, reloading data on every rotation.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified mvi-architecture lines 131-133: `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.onIntent(HomeIntent.LoadItems) }`. On configuration change the Activity/composition is recreated by default, so LaunchedEffect(Unit) enters composition fresh and re-runs, re-dispatching LoadItems. loadItems() (lines 84-96) then sets isLoading=true and re-fetches, replacing state.items on the already-populated (retained) ViewModel — a redundant reload/spinner flash per rotation. A ViewModel `init{}` block (as android-patterns line 107 uses) runs once and survives config change, avoiding this. Real behavior; the defect only manifests on config change and the fetch may be cheap if cached, so 'minor' is the correct severity.

missedIssues: Error-modeling inconsistency the finder missed: ahmed android-patterns/SKILL.md line 117 stores the raw throwable message directly in UI state (`.onFailure { error -> _state.update { it.copy(error = error.message, ...) } }`). This contradicts (a) ahmed's OWN mvi-architecture skill, which maps errors to a rich domain `ErrorState` sealed type via `mapError()` (lines 28-32, 98-103), and (b) rcosteira android-dev line 23 which mandates 'Errors: mapped to a domain type at the repository boundary — platform exceptions never leak past it'. ahmed android-patterns/SKILL.md line 100 injects `savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle` into the ViewModel constructor but never uses it anywhere in the shown example — a dead/unused constructor parameter in code presented as a recommended pattern.

Speculative/minor, but the finder did not examine the test's correctness at all.

Both are legitimately confirmable, but they are double-counted rather than independent findings.

result.depthComparison: rcosteira is by far the most detailed and actionable for this cluster: one router SKILL.md plus 21 reference files covering state-management, side-effects, performance/stability (five compiler stability classifications, strong-skipping, baseline profiles), three animation files, focus, lists/scrolling, a production crash playbook, composition-locals, theming, navigation (2 and 3), accessibility, multiplatform, platform-specifics, design-to-compose, and the experimental Styles API — with AOSP source-file citations, library version gates, and even an --init-script recipe for auditing repos you do not own. Its breadth is also its weakness: the extra code surface is where all the compilable/staleness bugs live. chris is the strongest for review discipline: 11 tightly-scoped, single-topic skills each with an explicit review procedure, decision tables, 'When NOT to apply', 'Common mistakes', 'Red flags during review', and 'rationalization vs reality' tables, plus cross-skill routing (recomposition-performance is a pure router). chris is narrower per file and omits crash/multiplatform/navigation/theming/a11y entirely, but its guidance is the cleanest and I found no broken code in it. ahmed is a single ~220-line quick-reference cheat sheet: correct but shallow basic snippets (hoisting, remember variants, slot, modifier, LaunchedEffect/DisposableEffect, Material3 theme, LazyColumn, animations) with no review procedure, no stability/performance depth, and slot defaults that lag current best practice. contradictionVerdicts.topic: How to scope Activity-lifetime dependencies (activityScope/KoinScopeComponent vs activityRetainedScope/AndroidScopeComponent)
contradictionVerdicts.reasoning: Verified in both files. ahmed koin-patterns lines 99-112 present `scope<MainActivity> { scoped { NavigationController() } }` with `class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity(), KoinScopeComponent { override val scope: Scope by activityScope() }` under a bare '## Scopes // Activity scope' heading, with no config-change caveat and no mention of activityRetainedScope. rcosteira koin lines 45-62 explicitly make `activityRetainedScope` (backed by the Activity's retained ViewModel, accessed via `AndroidScopeComponent`) the default for 'Survives configuration changes (the common case)', warns 'do not hand-roll createScope / close for this case', and relegates the plain `scope<T>` to 'Custom lifetime not tied to an Activity.' These are genuinely divergent recommended defaults for scoping dependencies to an Activity, using different APIs and different component interfaces, and both auto-trigger on `scoped { }`. Nuance: ahmed's activityScope is a real, valid Koin API (not itself wrong) and ahmed never explicitly claims config-change survival, so it is not a head-on 'A says X, B says not-X' claim contradiction — but as canonical guidance an agent would receive materially conflicting patterns for the same broad decision, so the conflict is real.

bugVerdicts.description: ahmed koin-patterns: 'Activity scope' via scope<MainActivity>/activityScope() loses state across configuration changes (should use activityRetainedScope for config-change survival).
bugVerdicts.reasoning: The underlying technical fact is correct: `activityScope()` (lines 108-109) binds the scope to the Activity instance lifecycle, so on rotation the Activity is destroyed, the scope closes, and `scoped { NavigationController() }` (line 103) is recreated, discarding held state. For a NavigationController (which typically holds back-stack state) this is a legitimate concern. However, this is NOT a compile/runtime defect — activityScope is a documented, valid Koin API behaving exactly as designed, and the skill never claims the scope survives config changes. So it is a missing-caveat / suboptimal-default issue rather than an unambiguous 'bug,' and the 'major' severity is overstated. It also heavily overlaps with the confirmed contradiction. Real underlying issue, but overstated as a definitive major bug -> PARTIAL.

bugVerdicts.description: ahmed kmp-di line 225: `single<UserService>(override = true) { ... }` uses the definition-level `override` parameter deprecated in Koin 3.2 and removed in Koin 4.x.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Verified at line 225. The named `override` parameter on `single`/`factory` definitions was deprecated when implicit last-wins overriding became the default (Koin 3.2, 2022) and the parameter was removed in Koin 4.0. Against a current koin-bom (which rcosteira assumes, line 8), `single<UserService>(override = true) { ... }` fails to compile because the parameter no longer exists; the modern approach is to declare the fake last or configure override at module level. ahmed pins only `${koinVersion}` (no version), so on Koin 3.x it would still compile (with deprecation), but teaching a removed API as of 2026 is a genuine defect. CONFIRMED (severity 'major' is slightly high for illustrative test code, but the technical claim holds).

bugVerdicts.description: ahmed kmp-di lines 184-186: ServiceLocator.get does an unchecked generic cast `services[key] as T` with no fail-fast for a missing key.

This is fragile 'manual DI alternative' example code, but the criticism (unsafe cast + no fail-fast) is accurate. CONFIRMED, minor.

## 1. Cross-cluster conflicts

**A. TOP — Re-imported rcosteira skills collide with the already-installed `kotlin@bilue-foundry` plugin.** No cluster considered the installed plugin as a duplication source, but it is the biggest conflict:
- **Direct name collision:** the data-layer cluster keeps rcosteira's **`android-data-layer`**, and `kotlin@bilue-foundry` **also ships `android-data-layer`**. Two same-named skills, both auto-triggering on native-Android data-layer code, would coexist in the user's environment.
